text: Venus is the hottest planet because of its air. It is wrapped in an extremely thick [[atmosphere|atmosphere]] made mostly of [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]]. Sunlight gets in and warms the ground. The warm ground gives off heat, but the thick air won't let it escape back to space.

This is called the greenhouse effect, and on Venus it has run out of control. The surface stays at about 465 °C everywhere, at the poles, on the night side and in the middle of the day. That's hotter than a pizza oven, and hot enough to melt lead.

st.prompt: Venus is almost twice as far from the Sun as Mercury. Which planet has the hotter surface?

st.reveal: Venus, by a long way. Its thick blanket of carbon dioxide traps heat so well that its surface stays around 465 °C, hotter than the sunny side of Mercury. Mercury has almost no air, so its heat escapes into space at night.

sec.t:
Venus is almost exactly the same size as Earth and made of similar rock. From far away, they could pass for twins. Up close, they couldn't be more different.

The air at Venus's surface presses down about 90 times harder than on Earth. Standing there would feel like being nearly a kilometre deep in the ocean. Clouds of sulphuric [[acid|acid]] cover the whole planet, so thick that you could never see the Sun clearly from the ground. Those bright clouds reflect so much sunlight that Venus is the brightest object in our night sky after the Moon.

Landing on Venus is one of the hardest jobs in space exploration. The Soviet Union kept trying. In 1970, Venera 7 became the first spacecraft to land on another planet and send back data, though only faintly, for about 20 minutes.

In 1982, Venera 13 landed and sent back the first colour pictures of the surface: flat, orange-brown rock under a yellowish sky. It survived for about two hours before the heat and pressure destroyed it. No lander has lasted longer.

Venus spins the opposite way to most planets, and very slowly. [[@space-weird-day-longer-year|One full turn takes 243 Earth days]], while its trip around the Sun takes 225. So one spin takes longer than one trip around the Sun. On Venus, the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east.

Nobody knows for sure why it spins backwards. One idea is that a giant collision long ago knocked it over. Another is that the Sun's pull on its thick air slowly changed its spin.

After years of attention on Mars, Venus is getting visitors again. In 2024, India's government approved the Venus Orbiter Mission, which [[@isro-missions|ISRO]] plans to launch towards the end of the 2020s to study its surface and air. NASA and the European Space Agency are also planning Venus missions.

In [[@hindi-language|Hindi]], Venus is Shukra, which gives Friday its name, Shukravaar. Because it shines so brightly near sunrise and sunset, Venus is often called the morning star or the evening star, even though it is a planet. You'd need a very tough [[@thermometer|thermometer]] to measure it up close, though.

text: A sea anemone looks like a flower but is an animal, a relative of [[@jellyfish-sting|jellyfish]] and corals. Its waving [[tentacle|tentacles]] are armed with thousands of tiny stinging cells that fire when a small fish touches them. Most small fish are stung, stunned and eaten.

Clownfish, also called anemonefish, are different. A thick coat of slime on their skin stops the stinging cells from firing, or at least stops them doing harm. So clownfish live inside the anemone, sleeping and sheltering among its tentacles, where few [[predator|predators]] dare to follow. In return, they keep the anemone clean, chase away fish that nibble it and feed it with their waste. Both animals do better together than apart.

st.reveal: The largest male changes into a female over a few weeks, and the next biggest young male becomes the breeding male. So in real life, Nemo's father would probably have become his mother.

sec.t:
Each stinging cell holds a coiled thread, like a tiny harpoon. When something touches it, the thread shoots out in a fraction of a second and injects [[venom|venom]].

Scientists think clownfish [[mucus|mucus]] avoids setting off these harpoons. Some studies suggest it lacks certain chemicals, such as particular sugars, that normally trigger a sting. Many clownfish also go through a careful routine when they meet a new anemone. They touch its tentacles briefly with their fins and belly, again and again, over minutes or hours. During this time, they may pick up some of the anemone's own mucus. After that, the anemone seems to treat them as part of itself.

Only about 10 of the more than 1,000 kinds of sea anemones host clownfish, and each kind of clownfish has favourite partners.

sec.h: A good deal on both sides
sec.t:
The clownfish gets a safe home, a nest site and scraps from the anemone's meals. The anemone benefits too. Clownfish chase away butterflyfish, which bite anemone tentacles. Their wriggling moves water through the tentacles, bringing fresh oxygen. Their droppings provide [[nutrient|nutrients]] for the anemone and for the tiny [[algae|algae]] that live inside its body.

This kind of partnership, where both sides gain, is called mutualism. [[@coral-reefs|Coral reefs]] are full of them.

sec.h: The biggest fish is the boss
sec.t:
A single anemone may house a little group of clownfish. The largest is always the female, and she's in charge. The second largest is the breeding male. The rest are smaller males that don't breed, waiting their turn.

All clownfish start life as males. If the female dies, the breeding male grows larger and changes into a female, and the biggest of the young males becomes the new breeding male. Scientists call this kind of switch protandry.

The female lays hundreds of eggs on a rock right next to the anemone. The male guards them, fanning them with his fins and removing any that go bad, until they hatch about a week later. The tiny babies drift away in the open sea before settling on a reef and searching for an anemone of their own.

{{story:pixar}}

In 2003, the [[@pixar|Pixar]] film *Finding Nemo* made clownfish famous worldwide. Demand for them as pets shot up, and many were caught from reefs. Today, many aquarium clownfish are bred in tanks instead. In Kerala, researchers at the Central Marine Fisheries Research Institute breed them so coastal families can earn money without taking fish from the wild.

Clownfish live on reefs around the [[@andaman|Andaman]] and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep and the Gulf of Mannar. Divers there often find them by first spotting an anemone.

Warm seas are a growing danger. When the water gets too hot, anemones, like corals, can lose the algae that live inside them and turn white. This [[@coral-bleaching|coral bleaching]] weakens the anemone, and a clownfish without a healthy host has nowhere safe to hide.

text: Every camera does the same basic job. Light bounces off the thing you are photographing and enters the camera through a small opening. A lens bends that light so it lands in a sharp, upside-down picture on a surface at the back.

In old cameras that surface was film, coated with chemicals that darkened where light hit them. In a [[@smartphones|phone]] or digital camera it is a [[sensor|sensor]], a chip covered with millions of tiny light-catchers. Each one measures how much light falls on it and turns that into a number. A computer inside the camera puts all those numbers together into the photo you see.

st.prompt: A camera sensor is covered in tiny colour filters. Which colour gets the most of them?

options.t: Green

Blue

st.reveal: Most sensors use a pattern with two green filters for every red and blue one. Our eyes are most sensitive to green light, so extra green detail makes photos look sharper to us.

myth: The more megapixels a camera has, the better its photos.

Megapixels only tell you how many dots make up the picture. The quality of the lens, the size of the sensor and how much light reaches it matter just as much, which is why a big camera with fewer megapixels can beat a phone with more.

sec.h: A dark room with a hole

sec.t:
Seeing the picture was easy. Keeping it was the hard part. Around 1826–27, the French inventor Nicéphore Niépce pointed a camera out of an upstairs window and coated a metal plate with a substance that hardened in light. The exposure took many hours. The blurry rooftops it shows are the oldest photograph that still survives.

Inventors soon found faster chemicals. By 1888, the American company Kodak was selling a simple box camera loaded with film. You took your pictures, posted the whole camera back, and they returned your prints. The story of those early years is in [[@photography-history|the history of photography]].

In 1975, a young Kodak engineer named Steven Sasson built the first digital camera. It was about the size of a toaster. Its pictures were 100 dots wide and 100 dots tall, and saving each one to tape took about 23 seconds.

Today's sensors hold millions of light-catchers, each one making one [[@pixels|pixel]] of the final image. On their own, they can only measure brightness, not colour. So each one sits under a tiny red, green or blue filter, laid out like a chessboard. The camera then works out the true colour of every dot by comparing it with its neighbours.

sec.h: Three controls that make a photo
sec.t:
Photographers juggle three settings. The **aperture** is the size of the opening, like your pupil getting wider in the dark. The **shutter** decides how long light is let in: a thousandth of a second [[@how-cameras-speed|freezes a cricket ball in the air]], while a few seconds turns car headlights into streaks. The third is how sensitive the sensor is set to be.

A phone makes all three choices for you in a blink. It often takes several shots at once and blends them, which is why phone photos can look bright even in a dim room. The [[@lenses-glasses|lens]] is still doing the oldest job of all: bending light to a point.

text: Toothpaste is a thick mix of a few simple things. There is a gentle scrubbing powder, often chalk or silica, to polish away the sticky film on teeth. There is water and a syrupy liquid to keep it moist, a gum to make it thick, a foaming agent, a sweet flavour like mint, and usually fluoride to make teeth stronger.

In a factory, giant mixers blend all of it under a [[vacuum|vacuum]] so no air bubbles get trapped. Then machines squirt the paste into tubes through the open bottom end, squash that end flat and seal it. A single machine can fill well over a hundred tubes a minute.

The stripes are painted on as the paste leaves the tube

st.reveal: The coloured pastes are fed into the tube together in layers. Toothpaste is so thick that it flows out like a solid rod, without stirring, so the stripes stay in place right to the end.

myth: The more toothpaste you use, the cleaner your teeth get.

The brushing does most of the cleaning, and fluoride works in small amounts. Dentists suggest a smear the size of a grain of rice for children under 3 and a pea-sized blob for ages 3 to 6. Swallowing large amounts of fluoride toothpaste is not good for children.
facts: a gentle scrubber, water, a thickener, a foaming agent, flavour and usually fluoride

sec.t:
The scrubbing part is the surprise. Calcium carbonate is the same stuff as chalk, limestone and seashells. Silica is a cousin of sand and quartz. Both are ground into a powder much finer than flour, fine enough to polish teeth without scratching the hard outer coat, the [[enamel|enamel]].

Toothpaste makers test how scratchy each paste is. Too rough, and over years it could wear teeth down. Too gentle, and it won't remove stains from tea, coffee or turmeric. So toothpaste is a careful balance, like using a very soft scrubber on a steel pan.

Fluoride is the real hero. Every day, [[acid|acid]] made by mouth [[bacteria|bacteria]] pulls tiny amounts of minerals out of your enamel. Fluoride helps put minerals back and makes the surface tougher against the next acid attack. In the 1950s, large studies in the United States showed that fluoride toothpaste and water cut tooth decay sharply, and fluoride toothpaste spread around the world.

That's also why dentists say to spit, not rinse, after brushing. A little fluoride left on the teeth keeps working.

People cleaned their teeth long before tubes existed. Ancient Egyptians used powders that included ash and crushed eggshells. Romans used crushed bones and shells. In India, people have chewed twigs of [[@neem|neem]] and babool for thousands of years. The frayed end works like a brush, and neem has bitter chemicals that bacteria dislike. Many Indian toothpastes still advertise neem, clove or salt.

The first toothpaste sold in jars appeared in the 1870s. In the 1890s, an American dentist named Washington Sheffield began selling toothpaste in squeezable metal tubes, borrowed from the tubes painters used for oil paint. Plastic tubes took over much later.

Most toothpaste tubes are made of thin layers of plastic and aluminium pressed together, which keeps the paste fresh but makes them very hard to recycle. Companies are now testing tubes made of one kind of plastic so they can be melted down and reused.

The paste itself is one of the last steps in keeping a mouth healthy. The other half is the brush, and the story of the [[@toothbrush|toothbrush]] goes back to a Chinese invention made with pig hair.

text: A photocopier makes a copy in a few seconds by using light, [[@static-electricity|static electricity]], a fine powder called toner, and heat.

Inside is a drum, a metal cylinder coated with a special material. First the drum is given a static charge all over. Then a bright light shines onto your page, and the light reflected off it falls on the drum. Wherever light hits, the charge leaks away. Only the dark parts, the shapes of the words and pictures, stay charged.
Toner powder sticks to those charged parts. The drum rolls the powder onto a sheet of paper, and hot rollers melt it in place. Out comes your copy, still warm.

st.prompt: Why does a fresh photocopy come out warm?

options.t: A hot roller melts the toner powder into the paper
The bright light inside heats the paper
The paper rubs on metal and gets hot from friction

st.reveal: Toner is a powder made mostly of tiny plastic grains. Hot rollers melt it so it soaks into the paper fibres and sets as it cools. Without that step, you could brush the words right off the page.

sec.t:
Before photocopiers, copying a document was slow. People retyped it, traced it, or used messy carbon paper, which made a faint copy as you typed.

Chester Carlson knew this first-hand. He worked in the patent office of an electronics company in New York, and he spent long days copying drawings and papers by hand. He also had arthritis, which made his hands hurt.

So he set out to invent a copying machine. He worked in his kitchen, and later in a small room behind a beauty salon in Astoria, a part of New York City.

On 22 October 1938, Carlson and his helper, Otto Kornei, wrote "10.-22.-38 ASTORIA." in ink on a glass slide. They rubbed a zinc plate coated with sulphur to give it a static charge, pressed the slide to it and shone a bright lamp on it.

Next they dusted the plate with a fine powder. The powder clung only where the writing had been. They pressed waxed paper onto it and warmed it. The words appeared on the paper. It was the world's first xerographic copy.

For years, more than 20 companies turned Carlson down. They thought carbon paper was good enough. Finally a small firm called Haloid agreed to develop his idea. It later renamed itself Xerox.

{{story:patents}}

In 1959 Xerox launched the 914, the first machine that could quickly make copies on ordinary paper at the press of a button. It weighed close to 300 kg and was too big to fit on a desk.

It could also overheat, and if paper got stuck near the hot parts, it might start to smoke or burn. So each machine came with a small fire extinguisher. Even so, offices loved it. Suddenly anyone could copy a letter in seconds. Xerox grew into a giant company, and "to xerox" came to mean "to photocopy" in many countries, including India.

Today's copiers work on the same idea, but with digital parts. A scanner bar with a row of tiny light [[sensor|sensors]] slides under the glass and turns the page into a digital image. Then a laser draws that image onto the charged drum, just as in a laser [[@printers|printer]]. In fact, many office machines are printer, scanner and copier in one.

Colour copiers use four toners: cyan, magenta, yellow and black. They lay down each colour in turn.

In India, the small "xerox shop" near schools, colleges and government offices is a familiar sight. Students copy notes, and families copy forms, ID cards and certificates.

Photocopiers changed how information spread. Before them, a rare book or document could be read only where it was kept, often in a [[@libraries|library]]. After them, pages could be copied and shared widely. Chester Carlson became rich from his invention and gave most of his fortune away to charities before he died in 1968.

text: A wind turbine is a windmill that makes electricity. Wind pushes on its long blades and makes them spin. The blades turn a shaft inside the box at the top, called the nacelle. Usually a gearbox speeds up the slow turning of the blades, which might spin only 10 to 20 times a minute, into the fast spin a generator needs.

The [[generator|generator]] is where movement becomes electricity. Inside it, [[@magnets-how|magnets]] spin past coils of copper wire, which makes [[electron|electrons]] flow in the wire. Thick cables carry the electricity down the tower and off to homes, schools and factories. A large modern turbine can make enough electricity for a few thousand Indian homes.

st.prompt: On a stormy day with very strong winds, what does a modern wind turbine usually do?

Turns its blades edge-on and stops to protect itself
Folds its blades down against the tower

st.reveal: Above a certain wind speed, often around 90 km/h, turbines turn their blades so the wind slips past and apply brakes. Spinning too fast could damage the blades and the machinery inside. They start again when the storm passes.

sec.h: From grinding grain to making power
sec.t:
People have used wind for thousands of years, to fill sails and to turn millstones that ground grain. Windmills with sails turning around an upright post were built in Persia, in present-day Iran, more than a thousand years ago, and some old ones still stand near the town of Nashtifan.

The first windmills to make electricity came in the 1880s. In the winter of 1887–88, an inventor named Charles Brush built a giant windmill in his back garden in Cleveland, Ohio. Its wooden rotor was 17 metres across, and it charged batteries in his basement that powered his house lights for about 20 years.

Turbines need steady, strong wind, so they are built on open plains, hilltops, coasts and out at sea. In India, the [[@extreme-windiest|windiest]] areas include the gaps in the Western Ghats in Tamil Nadu, and the coasts of Gujarat. Near Muppandal in Tamil Nadu, hundreds of turbines line the fields, catching wind that funnels through a pass in the hills. India is now among the top five countries in the world for wind power.

In the USA, [[@texas|Texas]] makes more electricity from wind than any other state. Offshore turbines, standing in the sea, can be even bigger, because ships can carry huge parts that would never fit on a road. Winds at sea are also steadier, with no hills or buildings to slow them down.

Wind turbines make no smoke or [[@climate-change|greenhouse gases]] while running, but they have downsides. The wind doesn't always blow, so turbines must work alongside other power sources and storage. Some people dislike the look and the swishing noise. Turbines can also kill birds and [[@bats-fly|bats]] that fly into the blades. Builders try to keep them away from [[@migration|migration]] routes, and some wind farms pause their turbines when large flocks pass. In Rajasthan, wind farms and their power lines are part of the danger facing the rare great Indian bustard.

text: कथकली केरल का नृत्य-नाटक है, और इसका मेकअप दुनिया के सबसे बारीक मेकअप में से एक है। प्रदर्शन से पहले कलाकार चटाई पर पीठ के बल लेट जाता है। मेकअप कारीगर उसके चेहरे पर गाढ़े रंग लगाता है, फिर जबड़े के साथ-साथ एक कान से दूसरे कान तक एक कड़ा सफ़ेद ढाँचा बनाता है, जिसे चुट्टी कहते हैं।

पूरे काम में अक्सर तीन-चार घंटे लगते हैं। [[pigment|रंग]] परंपरा से [[mineral|खनिजों]] और पौधों को पीसकर, नारियल के तेल में मिलाकर बनते थे। फिर आती है पोशाक: भारी-भरकम घेरदार घाघरे, वज़नी गहने और ऊँचा मुकुट।

ज़्यादातर कथकली कलाकार मर्द होते हैं, औरतों के किरदारों में भी, हालाँकि अब ज़्यादा औरतें भी मंच पर आती हैं। जब तक कलाकार उठकर खड़ा होता है, वह खुद गायब हो चुका होता है। उसकी जगह होता है कोई देवता, राजा या राक्षस।

हर रंग का एक काम है। दर्शक चेहरा वैसे ही पढ़ते हैं जैसे तुम ट्रैफ़िक की बत्ती पढ़ते हो।

- पच्चा, यानी हरा, कृष्ण, अर्जुन और नल जैसे नेक नायकों के लिए है।
- कत्ति, यानी छुरी, रावण जैसे घमंडी, ताकतवर खलनायकों के लिए है। चेहरा हरा होता है, गाल पर छुरी की धार की तरह ऊपर मुड़ती एक लाल धारी होती है, और नाक और माथे पर सफ़ेद गोले।
- ताड़ी, यानी दाढ़ी, तीन तरह की होती है। लाल दाढ़ी दुष्ट, हिंसक किरदारों के लिए। सफ़ेद दाढ़ी हनुमान जैसे अच्छे किरदारों के लिए। काली दाढ़ी शिकारियों और जंगल के लोगों के लिए।
- करि, यानी काला, राक्षसियों के लिए है।
- मिनुक्कु, यानी चमकीला, औरतों, ऋषियों और पुजारियों के लिए हल्का पीला-नारंगी रंग है।

कहानियाँ ज़्यादातर दो [[epic|महाकाव्यों]], [[@ramayana|रामायण]] और महाभारत, से आती हैं, इसलिए किरदारों में नायकों और खलनायकों की भरमार होती है।

चुट्टी सबसे ज़्यादा ध्यान खींचती है। परंपरा से यह चूने में मिले चावल के लेप से बनती थी, जिसे पतली परतों में लगाकर सूखते-सूखते आकार दिया जाता था। आज बहुत-सी मंडलियाँ इसे सफ़ेद कागज़ से काटकर चावल के लेप से चिपकाती हैं, जो जल्दी हो जाता है।

कारीगर धीरे-धीरे, एक-एक उभार बनाते हुए काम करता है, जब तक ढाँचा गाल से कई सेंटीमीटर बाहर न निकल आए। इससे चेहरा एक चमकती आकृति बन जाता है, जो खुले में बैठी भीड़ की आखिरी कतार से भी दिख जाए। यह ज़रूरी था, क्योंकि कभी प्रदर्शन पीतल के एक बड़े तेल के दीये की रोशनी में पूरी रात चलते थे।

प्रदर्शन खत्म होने पर चुट्टी टुकड़ों में उतार ली जाती है और नारियल के तेल से रंग रगड़कर छुड़ाए जाते हैं। घंटों की मेहनत मिनटों में गायब हो जाती है, और अगली रात सब फिर से शुरू होता है।

कथकली कलाकार बरसों तक अपनी आँखों का अभ्यास करते हैं। वे उन्हें घुमाना, झटके से फेरना और हर भौं को अलग से नचाना सीखते हैं। आँखों को और भी नाटकीय दिखाने के लिए कुछ कलाकार निचली पलक के नीचे चुंडप्पू पौधे का एक नन्हा बीज रख लेते हैं। इससे प्रदर्शन के दौरान आँख का सफ़ेद हिस्सा लाल हो जाता है।

मेकअप उसी चेहरे को उभारने के लिए बनाया जाता है। [[@art-masks-world|मुखौटे]] के उलट, यह हर फड़कन के साथ हिलता है, इसलिए उठी हुई भौं या गाल की कँपकँपी भी दर्शकों तक पहुँच जाती है।

कथकली 1600 के दशक में केरल में पनपी, कुछ हद तक रामनाट्टम नाम के एक पुराने मंदिर-नाटक से। 1900 के दशक की शुरुआत तक इसे सहारा मिलना कम हो गया था। 1930 में कवि वल्लतोल नारायण मेनन ने केरल कलामंडलम की स्थापना में मदद की, एक ऐसा विद्यालय जिसने नर्तकों और मेकअप कारीगरों की एक नई पीढ़ी तैयार की।

वहाँ विद्यार्थी बरसों पढ़ते हैं। मेकअप कारीगर उस्तादों को देखते हुए शागिर्द बनकर सीखते हैं, और तभी किसी असली चेहरे पर हाथ लगाने का मौका पाते हैं। कई सबसे अच्छे कलाकारों ने दस साल की उम्र में ही प्रशिक्षण शुरू कर दिया था।

कथकली पेरिस से न्यूयॉर्क तक दुनिया घूम चुकी है। फिर भी [[@kerala|केरल]] के किसी मंदिर के आँगन में प्रदर्शन आज भी पुराने ढंग से, ढोल और दीये के साथ शुरू होता है। और सबसे मज़े की बात? कलाकार आँखों से जिस तरह बात करते हैं, वह अपने आप में एक पूरी भाषा है, जिसका राज़ [[@kathakali|कथकली चेहरों से कहानियाँ कैसे सुनाती है]] में खुलता है।

text: Warli art is a style of painting made by the Warli people. They are an Adivasi (tribal) community who live mostly in the hills and forests north of [[@mumbai|Mumbai]], in Maharashtra. For generations they have painted white figures on the reddish-brown [[@art-lippan|mud walls]] of their homes.

The paintings are built from three basic shapes. A circle can be the sun, the moon or a head. A triangle can be a mountain, a tree or half a body. A square marks out a sacred space. From these, painters create busy scenes of farming, hunting, festivals and dancing, full of tiny people who seem to be on the move.

st.reveal: A Warli person is two triangles touching tip to tip, like an hourglass, with stick arms and legs and a round head. Tilt the triangles and the person seems to dance or walk.

The shapes are simple on purpose, but each one carries meaning, and arranging hundreds of tiny figures so the whole scene moves takes years of practice. Warli painters also follow rules about what goes where, especially in wedding paintings.

sec.t:
Warli painting began as a [[ritual|ritual]] art, and its most important use is at a wedding. Married women of the community would paint a square called a *chauk* on the wall of the house. Inside it they drew Palaghata, a goddess linked with fertility and a good harvest.

Around the chauk spread scenes of everyday village life: people carrying water, a bullock cart, birds in trees, a man climbing a palm. The painting brought blessings to the couple, and it also recorded how the community lived, much like a family photo album on a wall.

sec.h: The tarpa dance in a circle
sec.t:
One scene turns up again and again. Dozens of dancers hold hands in a great spiral, curling inwards around a musician who plays the *tarpa*, a long wind instrument made from a dried gourd. The Warli dance this way at harvest time.

Painters show the spiral with tiny figures that get smaller towards the centre. It works a bit like a whirlpool: your eye gets pulled round and round. [[@circles|Circles]] matter in Warli thinking because life, the [[@seasons-why|seasons]] and the dance all turn in loops, with no real beginning or end. You can see a similar love of balanced patterns in [[@rangoli-symmetry|rangoli]] drawn on doorsteps across India.

sec.h: From village walls to the world
sec.t:
For centuries hardly anyone outside the Warli villages saw these paintings. That changed in the 1970s, when an artist named Jivya Soma Mashe began painting Warli scenes on paper and cloth instead of walls. His work was shown in galleries in India and abroad, and he received the Padma Shri in 2011.

Today Warli designs appear on saris, mugs, railway station walls and school notebooks. This has brought income to some Warli artists, but it has also raised a worry. When factories print the patterns cheaply, the people whose tradition it is may earn nothing. Like [[@madhubani|Madhubani painting]] from Bihar, Warli art now has a legal tag that links the name to the community.

Warli scenes remind many people of the hunters and dancers painted on [[@art-cave-paintings-bhimbetka|rock shelters at Bhimbetka]], which are thousands of years old. Some writers suggest the style may descend from that kind of [[@cave-art|ancient rock painting]]. It is a tempting idea, but it is hard to prove, because mud walls crumble and very old Warli paintings simply have not survived. What is certain is that the style has been handed down from parent to child for a very long time, without ever needing a pencil or a printed guide.

text: Doctors find out what is wrong with people and help them get better or stay well. A lot of that is detective work. They ask questions, listen, examine the body and order tests like blood tests or X-rays. Then they decide on a treatment and explain it.

But there is no single doctor's day. A family doctor in a small town might see 40 patients in a morning, most with coughs, fevers and aches. A [[surgeon|surgeon]] might spend six hours on one operation. A doctor in a village health centre might be the only one for many kilometres. All of them also write notes, sign forms and talk to worried families.

sec.t:
In a [[@hospitals|hospital]], many doctors start the day with ward rounds. A senior doctor walks from bed to bed with a team of junior doctors, nurses and students. At each bed they check how the patient slept, look at charts and test results, and decide what happens next.

Rounds are also how young doctors learn. A senior might ask a student to explain why a patient's temperature rose overnight. Then the team plans the day: who needs a scan, who can go home, who needs a specialist.

Doctors have a saying: listen to the patient, and they will tell you what is wrong. How a pain started, what makes it worse, whether others at home are sick: these clues often matter more than any machine.

Then comes the examination. A stethoscope lets a doctor hear the heart and lungs. A torch shows the back of the throat. A tap on the knee tests the [[@reflexes|reflexes]]. Only after this do most doctors decide which tests are worth doing. Good doctors also say "I don't know yet" when that's the truth.

After basic training, many doctors specialise. Paediatricians look after children. Cardiologists treat hearts, and surgeons operate. Radiologists read X-rays and scans. Psychiatrists care for mental health. Some surgeons now work with [[@robots-surgery|robots]] that hold tools steadier than any human hand.

Becoming a doctor takes a long time. In India, students sit an entrance exam called NEET, then study for about 5½ years for an MBBS degree, including a year as an intern. Many then train for three more years in a specialty. In the US, students usually finish a four-year college degree first, then four years of medical school, then three to seven years of hospital training.

Illness doesn't keep office hours, so hospitals need doctors around the clock. Young doctors often work long night shifts. They also see sad things, and learning to cope with that is part of the job.

Doctors work in teams. Nurses, pharmacists, lab technicians and ambulance crews do much of the care a patient receives. In India, people like the surgeon [[@sushruta|Sushruta]], who described operations about 2,000 years ago, are remembered as early teachers of medicine. India celebrates National Doctors' Day on 1 July, the birthday of Dr B. C. Roy, a doctor who also became chief minister of West Bengal.

text: A national park is land a country protects so that wild nature isn't cut down, built over or hunted out. People can still visit, learn and enjoy it, but the plants and animals come first.

In 1872, the USA made [[@usa-wonder-yellowstone|Yellowstone]] the world's first national park, to protect its [[@old-faithful|geysers]], forests and animals. Since then, almost every country has created parks of its own.
Parks protect more than pretty views. They keep forests that store water, rivers that supply towns, and animals that might otherwise vanish.

sec.t:
In the 1860s and 1870s, explorers came back from the Yellowstone region, in today's Wyoming, Montana and Idaho, with stories of boiling springs and water shooting into the sky. Some people didn't believe them.

[[expedition|Expeditions]] brought back paintings and photographs. Congress was convinced, and on 1 March 1872, President Ulysses S. Grant signed a law making Yellowstone a "public park or pleasuring-ground for the benefit and enjoyment of the people". It was a new idea: land owned by the nation and kept wild for everyone.

India's first national park opened in 1936 in the hills of today's [[@uttarakhand|Uttarakhand]]. It was called Hailey National Park, and is now [[@kipling-india|Jim Corbett]] National Park. Corbett had once hunted tigers that attacked people, then spent his later life writing and campaigning to protect them.

Today India has more than 100 national parks, including Kaziranga in Assam for [[@rhino-kaziranga|one-horned rhinos]] and Gir in Gujarat, the only home of wild Asiatic lions. Hemis in [[@ladakh|Ladakh]] shelters snow leopards high in the mountains.

India also has hundreds of wildlife [[sanctuary|sanctuaries]]. The difference is about rules. In a national park, activities like grazing cattle or collecting firewood are usually not allowed. In a sanctuary, some local uses may be permitted.

Some special areas are tiger reserves, biosphere reserves or [[@marine-parks-india|marine parks]]. The Gulf of Mannar, between India and Sri Lanka, protects [[@coral-reefs|coral reefs]], sea grass and dugongs under the water.

Millions of people visit national parks every year. In the USA, Great Smoky Mountains is the most visited. In India, jeep safaris in parks like [[@ranthambore|Ranthambore]] and Kanha are popular.

Visitors bring money and jobs to nearby villages, but too many vehicles and too much noise can disturb animals. Many parks limit how many vehicles can enter each day, and close core areas during the [[monsoon|monsoon]].

Some parks were made on land where people already lived, and those families had to move. Native American tribes lost land when some US parks were created. In India, forest-dwelling communities have sometimes been moved out of reserves.

Today, many parks try to work with local communities, not against them. India's Forest Rights Act of 2006 recognises the rights of forest dwellers. Former hunters and village youth often work as guides and guards, and nobody knows the forest better.

text: In much of India, grandparents have traditionally lived with their grown-up children, usually a son, in a joint family. Children grew up with grandparents in the next room. The young cared for the old, and the old helped raise the young.

That pattern is still common. Most Indians over 60 live with family. But it is changing. Many young people move to cities or abroad for work, families are smaller, and people are living longer. More grandparents now live alone or as a couple, and families rely more on pensions, video calls, neighbours, paid carers and, sometimes, old-age homes.

sec.t:
A joint family brings several generations under one roof: grandparents, their sons, their sons' wives and children, and sometimes unmarried daughters and other relatives. Elders were often respected as heads of the household. Many Indian traditions, across religions, stress caring for parents as a duty.

In this system, grandparents are much more than people to be cared for. They cook, tell stories, teach prayers and recipes, watch the children while parents work and pass on family history. A lot of [[@storytelling-india|Indian storytelling]] has been handed down at grandparents' knees.

In villages across India, many young people move to cities for work. Some go abroad, to the Gulf countries, the US or Europe. Their parents often stay behind, especially in places like Kerala, where so many people work overseas that some villages are mostly older people.

Phones help. Grandparents video-call grandchildren they see only once a year. Children send money home. But a phone can't take someone to the doctor at night. Neighbours, local doctors and community groups often fill the gap.

Many older Indians, especially women and farm workers, never had a job with a pension. The government pays a small monthly [[@pensions-old-age|old-age pension]] to poor elders through the Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme, with states adding their own money.

In 2007, India passed a law making children responsible for supporting their elderly parents. A parent who is neglected can ask a tribunal to order the children to pay a monthly allowance. There is also a free national helpline for senior citizens, Elderline, on the number 14567.

Old-age homes exist in most cities, run by charities, religious groups and companies. For some families they bring a sense of shame. Others see them as a way for elders to get daily care and company.

sec.h: How it works in the US
sec.t:
In the United States, most older people live on their own or with a husband or wife, not with grown-up children. Many receive Social Security, a government pension started in 1935. Some move to retirement communities or nursing homes.

But multigenerational living is growing there too, partly because of high housing costs and partly because of immigrant families, including many [[@indian-diaspora|Indian-American]] ones, who bring the habit of living together. In both countries, families are working out new ways to look after people who once looked after them.

text: The police keep people safe and help make sure laws are followed. They patrol streets, respond to emergencies, investigate crimes, manage traffic, find missing people, and help at big crowds like festivals and cricket matches.

Police can arrest people they believe have broken the law, but they cannot punish them. Deciding guilt and punishment is the job of [[@courts-judges|judges]]. That split matters: it stops any single group from having too much power over people's lives.

sec.t:
In India, [[@constitution|the Constitution]] makes police a state subject. So the Kerala Police, the Maharashtra Police and others are separate forces run by state governments. Senior officers usually come from the Indian Police Service, recruited nationally.

In the United States, policing is even more local. Cities, counties and states run their own forces, and there are thousands of separate police departments. National agencies like the FBI handle certain serious crimes that cross state lines.

Many cities had watchmen for centuries, but the first modern, uniformed police force is often traced to [[@london|London]]. Home Secretary Robert Peel set up the Metropolitan Police in 1829. Londoners nicknamed the officers "bobbies" or "peelers" after him, and the first name is still used.

In India, the British passed the Police Act of 1861 after the [[@revolt-1857|revolt of 1857]]. Much of the structure of Indian policing still dates from that law, and many experts say it needs updating.

Police detectives gather evidence: CCTV footage, phone records, witness statements and [[@fingerprints|fingerprints]]. In 1897, the British official Edward Henry set up the world's first [[@fingerprint-sensors|fingerprint bureau]] in Calcutta, now [[@kolkata|Kolkata]]. Two Indian officers, Azizul Haque and Hem Chandra Bose, worked out much of the system for sorting prints so they could be found quickly. Versions of it were used around the world for about a century.

For a long time, police forces were almost entirely male. In 1972, Kiran Bedi became the first woman to join the Indian Police Service. Today many Indian states have reserved a share of police posts for women and run all-women police stations, where women can report crimes more comfortably.

Most police work is not chasing criminals. Officers spend much of their time answering calls, sorting out arguments, helping at accidents and guiding traffic. Before electric signals, police stood at crossings and waved cars through by hand.

{{story:traffic-lights}}

Police uniforms in India are usually khaki, a word that means "dust-coloured" in Persian and Hindi. British Indian army units began dyeing their uniforms this colour in the 1840s because it blended into dusty ground, and police forces later took it up. Many American police wear dark blue instead, a colour that goes back to early forces in cities like New York.

Emergency numbers make it easy to call for help. The first 911 call in the US was made in Haleyville, Alabama, in 1968. India now uses 112 for police, fire and ambulance together.

Police have special powers, so they must follow strict rules. People have [[@rights-duties|rights]] when they are stopped or arrested, such as being told why. In both India and the USA there have been serious complaints about police misusing force or treating some groups unfairly. Courts, human rights commissions, body cameras and community policing are all ways societies try to keep police honest. Policing tends to work best when people trust officers enough to report problems and help with investigations.

text: Yes. In 1989, countries agreed on the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, a [[treaty|treaty]] listing the rights every person under 18 should have. Almost every country in the world has joined it.

It says children have the right to be safe, to go to school, to [[@universal-healthcare|health care]], to play and rest, and to have a say in decisions that affect them. Grown-ups and governments must put children's best interests first.
India's Right to Education Act (2009) says every child aged 6–14 should get free schooling. Rights come with respect: your rights matter, and so do everyone else's.

sec.t:
A hundred years ago, most countries had few laws protecting children. Many worked long hours in mines, factories and fields. After the [[@world-war-one|First World War]], a British teacher named Eglantyne Jebb founded Save the Children to help hungry children in Europe.

In 1923 she wrote a short declaration of children's rights. The League of Nations, the body before the [[@united-nations|United Nations]], adopted it in 1924. It was only a few lines long, but it planted an idea that grew.

Indian law says every child from 6 to 14 has the right to free and compulsory education. This was added to the [[@constitution|Constitution]] in 2002, and the Right to Education Act followed in 2009. Private schools must keep a quarter of their entry-class seats for children from poorer families.

Free school meals, like India's [[@mid-day-meal|mid-day meal]] scheme, help too. Hungry children find it hard to learn, and many families send children to school partly because of the lunch.

No child should be hurt or made to do dangerous work. Campaigners like [[@kailash-satyarthi|Kailash Satyarthi]] have spent decades freeing children from factories and quarries. Indian law bans employing children under 14 in almost all jobs.

In the USA, a 1938 law limited [[@child-labour|child labour]] across the country, after years of campaigning against children working in mills and mines.

Children have the right to share their views on things that affect them, and adults should take those views seriously. That might mean a student council at school, or a judge asking a child where they want to live after their parents separate.

Young people around the world have used this voice. [[@malala|Malala Yousafzai]] spoke out for girls' schooling in Pakistan when she was just 11.

In India, any child in trouble can call 1098 for free, day or night, for help. Trusted adults, such as teachers, parents and doctors, are there to help too. Knowing your rights is the first step towards making sure they are respected, for you and for every child around you.

text: Dominoes look like a simple game, but they are packed with maths. Counting the tiles in a set leads to triangular numbers. Covering a board with dominoes leads to the Fibonacci pattern and to puzzles that seem impossible until you spot the trick. And a falling line of dominoes is a lesson in energy, the same idea mathematicians use to prove things go on forever.
All you need to explore it is a box of tiles, or some rectangles cut from card.

st.reveal: For strips 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 long, the answers are 1, 2, 3, 5 and 8. Each number is the sum of the two before it, the famous Fibonacci pattern.

myth: A falling domino can only knock over one the same size or smaller.
Experiments show one domino can topple another about one and a half times its size. A growing chain multiplies that, so small pushes can end up toppling big blocks.

sec.t:
A standard set goes from blank-blank up to six-six. Each tile is a pair of numbers from 0 to 6, and no pair repeats. How many tiles is that?

Start with the tiles that include a six. There are seven: six with 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. Then the tiles with a five but no six: six of them. Keep going and you add 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 28. Numbers made this way are called triangular numbers, because you can arrange that many dots into a triangle. A double-nine set follows the same rule and has 55 tiles.

Here's a famous puzzle. A [[@chess-india|chessboard]] has 64 squares, and 32 dominoes cover it perfectly. Now cut off two opposite corners, leaving 62 squares. Can 31 dominoes cover what's left?

People try for ages. The answer is no, and colour shows why. Every domino covers one black and one white square. But the two cut corners are the same colour, so the board now has 32 squares of one colour and 30 of the other. No arrangement can ever work. A clever idea replaced hours of trying.

Stand a domino upright and it stores a little energy, because its centre is raised. Tip it, and [[@gravity-fall|gravity]] turns that into movement, enough to push over the next one. In 1983 the physicist Lorne Whitehead showed a domino can topple one about 1.5 times bigger.

That multiplies quickly. Fifteen dominoes, each 1.5 times taller than the last and starting at 5 millimetres, would end with one almost 1.5 metres high. Twenty-nine would end with a domino more than 400 metres tall, in theory. Physicists have built real chains like this, and the tiny first push is barely a nudge with a fingertip.

Mathematicians use dominoes to explain a way of proving things called induction. Show that the first domino falls. Then show that whenever one falls, it knocks the next. Together, those two facts prove every domino in an endless line falls, without checking them one by one.

Dominoes themselves came from [[@ancient-china|ancient China]], where they were recorded about 800 years ago and often had pips for dice rolls. They reached Europe in the 1700s. Their cousins, shapes made of four squares, became famous in 1984 when a Soviet computer scientist used them to make Tetris, a game about filling gaps, which is a cousin of [[@tessellations|tessellations]].

In the USA it is usually called soccer, because "football" there means [[@american-football|American football]], a different game where players mostly carry and throw an oval ball. That's almost all you need to start. The full rule book, called the Laws of the Game, has 17 laws. It covers the pitch, the ball, fouls, offside, free kicks and penalties.

sec.h: The pitch, the ball and the clock
sec.t:
A pitch for international matches is 100 to 110 metres long and 64 to 75 metres wide, big enough to hold more than 25 tennis courts. The ball is about 70 cm around and weighs about 430 grams, close to three cricket balls.

The referee keeps time. Stoppages for injuries, substitutions and goal celebrations are added at the end of each half, which is why you see "+4" on the screen. Each team may make up to five substitutions in a normal match. In knockout games that end level, there may be 30 minutes of extra time and then a penalty shoot-out.

sec.t:
A foul is an unfair act, such as tripping, pushing or handling the ball. The other team gets a free kick. If a defender fouls inside their own penalty area, the attackers get a penalty: one shot from 11 metres with only the goalkeeper to beat.

For bad fouls the referee shows a yellow card as a warning. A second yellow, or one very serious foul, brings a red card, and the player must leave. Their team plays the rest of the match with one person fewer, which is a big handicap on a pitch that size. The cards were the idea of Ken Aston, an English referee. He saw how confusing spoken warnings were at the 1966 World Cup, and thought of the idea while stopped at a traffic light. They were first used at the 1970 World Cup in Mexico.

People kicked balls around in many countries for centuries, but each school or town had its own rules. In 1863, a group of clubs met in a London pub and formed the Football Association, which wrote the first shared rules.

British soldiers and traders carried the game around the world, including to India. In 1911, Mohun Bagan played barefoot against the East Yorkshire Regiment in the IFA Shield final in [[@kolkata|Kolkata]], and won 2–1. Huge crowds turned out, and the win became a symbol of Indian pride. Today, more countries play football than any other team sport. The 2026 [[@fifa-world-cup|World Cup]], in the USA, Canada and Mexico, was the first with 48 teams, and Spain won it by beating Argentina 1–0.

He was famous for flying dunks, clutch shots in the last seconds and a fierce will to win. His Nike shoe, the Air Jordan, became one of the best-selling sports products ever. To many people around the world in the 1990s, he was the face of America's [[@nba|NBA]].

sec.t:
Jordan was born in Brooklyn, New York, in 1963 and grew up in Wilmington, North Carolina. At Laney High School, at 15, he tried out for the varsity team and was sent to junior varsity instead. Coaches wanted a taller player.

He went home upset and then practised harder. He grew taller too, and made the varsity team the next year. In 1982, as a first-year student at the University of North Carolina, he hit the winning shot in the national college championship final.

For years Jordan scored huge numbers of points, but the Bulls could not win the championship. Under coach Phil Jackson, with teammate Scottie Pippen, they finally won in 1991, then again in 1992 and 1993.

In 1992 Jordan played on the US Olympic "Dream Team" in Barcelona, with Magic Johnson and Larry Bird. They won every game by big margins, and children around the world wanted to play basketball. It was the first Olympics where NBA professionals were allowed to play, and opponents sometimes asked the Americans for photos after losing to them.

In October 1993, after his father was killed in a robbery, Jordan retired from basketball. He then played minor-league baseball for the Birmingham Barons, a dream his father had shared. He worked hard but struggled as a hitter.

In March 1995 he returned to the Bulls with a two-word message: "I'm back." The Bulls won 72 of 82 games in 1995–96, a record at the time. They went on to win three more titles from 1996 to 1998. In the 1997 Finals he played while sick with what was called flu and still scored 38 points.

Jordan retired again in 1999, returned to play for the Washington Wizards from 2001 to 2003, then stopped for good. For more than a decade he was the main owner of the Charlotte Hornets, an NBA team in his home state.

He has been criticised at times for being very harsh on teammates. A 2020 documentary series, *The Last Dance*, showed both his drive and his toughness, and introduced him to a new generation who had never seen him play live.

text: Children thousands of years ago played many games we would recognise. They spun tops, threw pebbles and bones, rolled marbles and played chasing games. They had dolls, whistles, toy animals on wheels and board games with dice.

[[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] find these things in old houses, rubbish heaps and tombs. A toy cart from the [[@indus-cities|Indus cities]], more than 4,000 years old, would not look strange in a child's hands today. Some games have hardly changed at all. Others vanished for centuries and were only worked out again by scholars reading ancient rule books.

sec.t:
In the 1920s, the archaeologist Leonard Woolley dug up the royal tombs of Ur, a city in Mesopotamia, in modern Iraq. Among the gold and jewels were wooden boards decorated with shell and red and blue stone. Each had 20 squares in an odd shape, like two blocks joined by a narrow bridge.

It was a race game for two players, but the rules were lost. Then Irving Finkel, a curator at the British Museum, translated a clay tablet written by a Babylonian scribe in 177 BCE that explained how to play. Today you can play the Royal Game of Ur again, and museum visitors often do. Finkel also found that Jewish families in Kochi, Kerala, played a version of it into the 20th century.

sec.h: Games in the tombs of pharaohs

sec.t:
At Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, archaeologists have found thousands of small clay objects: bulls with nodding heads, toy carts with wheels, bird-shaped whistles, marbles and rattles. They also found cubic dice with dots from one to six, a little different in arrangement from ours.

Some of these may have had religious or adult uses. But many are small and cheerful, the kind of thing made for a child to push, blow or shake.

India has a long history of board games. Pachisi, a race game played on a cross-shaped cloth with cowrie shells as dice, was a royal favourite. At Fatehpur Sikri, a courtyard is laid out like a giant pachisi board, and stories say the emperor Akbar played using people as pieces. A simpler version reached Britain and became [[@ludo|ludo]].

[[@snakes-ladders|Snakes and ladders]] began in India as a game about life. Ladders were good deeds that lifted you up, and snakes were bad deeds that dragged you down. Chess grew from an Indian game called chaturanga, about 1,500 years ago.

Many of the oldest games needed nothing you had to buy. Five stones, or knucklebones, was played in ancient Greece with sheep's ankle bones, and Indian children still play it with pebbles, under names such as gutte. Hopscotch, tug of war and kite flying are all centuries old, and the yo-yo appears on Greek vases painted about 2,500 years ago.

In Indian villages, [[@sport-gilli-danda|gilli danda]] needs just two pieces of wood: a long stick and a short one tapered at both ends. Strike the short one so it flips up, then whack it as far as you can. Some historians think it may share an ancestor with cricket and baseball, though nobody can prove it.

इनेमल किसी भी [[@bones|हड्डी]] से सख़्त है। यह लगभग पूरी तरह कैल्शियम वाले एक [[crystal|क्रिस्टल]] जैसे खनिज से बना है। पर इसकी एक कमज़ोरी है: तेज़ाब। नींबू का रस, [[@soft-drinks|कोल्ड ड्रिंक]] और प्लाक के बैक्टीरिया का तेज़ाब, सब इसे नरम कर सकते हैं।

हड्डी के उलट, एक बार छेद हो जाए तो इनेमल फिर से नहीं उगता। जिन कोशिकाओं ने इसे बनाया था, वे दाँत के मुँह में निकलने से पहले ही ग़ायब हो जाती हैं। इसीलिए कैविटी को दाँतों के डॉक्टर से साफ़ करवाकर भरवाना पड़ता है। हाँ, तुम्हारे [[@teeth|दाँत]] बहुत शुरुआती नुकसान की मरम्मत लार के खनिजों से कर सकते हैं, ख़ासकर फ़्लोराइड की मदद से।

sec.h: फ़्लोराइड और मिशिगन का एक शहर
sec.t:
1900 के दशक की शुरुआत में अमेरिका के कोलोराडो में फ़्रेडरिक मैके नाम के एक दाँतों के डॉक्टर ने देखा कि बहुत-से स्थानीय लोगों के दाँतों पर भूरे दाग़ थे, पर हैरानी की बात यह कि कैविटी बहुत कम थीं। बरसों की जासूसी के बाद पता चला कि दोनों बातों की जड़ फ़्लोराइड है, एक खनिज जो उनके पानी में कुदरती रूप से मौजूद था।

1945 में मिशिगन का ग्रैंड रैपिड्स दुनिया का पहला शहर बना, जिसने अपने नल के पानी में सावधानी से थोड़ा-सा फ़्लोराइड मिलाया। वहाँ के बच्चों में कैविटी तेज़ी से घट गईं। आज ज़्यादातर [[@made-toothpaste|टूथपेस्ट]] में फ़्लोराइड होता है, जो इनेमल को फिर से बनने और तेज़ाब का सामना करने में मदद करता है। बहुत ज़्यादा फ़्लोराइड भी मुसीबत है। भारत के जिन इलाकों में ज़मीन के पानी में यह बहुत ज़्यादा है, वहाँ यह दाँतों पर दाग़ डाल सकता है और हड्डियों को नुकसान पहुँचा सकता है।

लोग हज़ारों साल से दाँतों की सड़न झेलते आए हैं। यह तब बहुत बढ़ गई जब [[@farming-began|खेती शुरू हुई]] और लोग स्टार्च वाले अनाज ज़्यादा खाने लगे, और फिर तब, जब कुछ सौ साल पहले सस्ती [[@sugar|चीनी]] दुनिया भर में फैल गई।

आज के पाकिस्तान में मेहरगढ़ नाम के एक प्राचीन खेतिहर गाँव में [[archaeologist|पुरातत्वविदों]] को लगभग 7,500 से 9,000 साल पुराने ऐसे दाँत मिले, जिनमें सफ़ाई से छेद किए गए थे, शायद चकमक पत्थर की नोक वाले औज़ारों से। पूरे भारत में लोग लंबे समय से [[@neem|नीम]] या बबूल की दातुन से दाँत साफ़ करते आए हैं। आज का नायलॉन वाला [[@toothbrush|टूथब्रश]] 1930 के दशक में आया। दिन में दो बार फ़्लोराइड वाले टूथपेस्ट से ब्रश करना और नियम से दाँतों के डॉक्टर को दिखाना, तेज़ाब बनाने वालों को काबू में रखने के सबसे अच्छे तरीके हैं।

text: A 3D printer makes a solid object by adding material one thin layer at a time. The most common kind for homes and schools pulls in a long thread of plastic, melts it in a hot nozzle at around 200 °C and squeezes it out like [[@made-toothpaste|toothpaste]]. The nozzle moves around, drawing the outline of one layer. The plastic cools and hardens in seconds.

Then the platform drops a fraction of a millimetre, or the nozzle rises, and the printer draws the next layer on top. Stack a few hundred of those and you have a toy, a phone stand or a spare part for a broken fan.

st.prompt: A home 3D printer is making a toy car about the size of your palm. Roughly how long might it take?

options.t: An hour or more
About ten seconds
About as long as printing a page of paper

st.reveal: Because the printer builds hundreds of thin layers one after another, even a small object can take an hour or several. Large or detailed objects can take a whole day.

sec.h: From a drawing to a stack of slices
sec.t:
Every print starts as a 3D drawing on a computer, a little like a [[@sculpture|digital sculpture]]. A program then cuts that drawing into hundreds of flat slices, each perhaps 0.2 mm thick. For each slice, it writes instructions telling the nozzle exactly where to go.

Hollow parts are a puzzle. A printer cannot lay plastic on thin air, so for overhangs it builds thin supports underneath, which you snap off later. Inside, objects are often not solid but filled with a honeycomb pattern. That saves plastic and time while keeping the object strong.

Bigger printers work with tougher stuff. Some fire a laser at fine metal powder to melt it into shape, making parts for [[@plane-jet|jet engines]] and rockets. In 2024, the Chennai company Agnikul Cosmos launched a small test [[@rockets-how|rocket]] whose engine was 3D-printed as one single piece.

Others print with [[@cement-concrete|concrete]]. In 2023 a post office in Cambridge Layout, [[@bengaluru|Bengaluru]], opened with walls printed by a giant machine that squeezed out concrete in curving layers. It took weeks, not the many months a normal building might take. Printed walls can curve easily, because the machine doesn't care whether it is drawing a straight line or a wavy one. In the United States, companies have used the same method to print whole houses in Texas.

Astronauts can't pop to a shop if a tool breaks. In 2014, a 3D printer on the [[@space-station|International Space Station]] made its first object, a small part for the printer itself. Since then astronauts have printed tools and spare parts. Future crews on the [[@mars-colonies|Moon or Mars]] might print shelters using local dust and rock.

[[@jobs-doctor|Doctors]] use 3D printing too. They print models of a patient's heart or bones to plan an operation, and make [[@prosthetics|artificial hands and legs]] shaped to fit one person exactly. A plastic printer in a classroom works on the same idea as all of these: slice it, then stack it.

text: Most of today's rechargeable [[@batteries|batteries]], in phones, laptops and [[@electric-cars|electric cars]], are lithium-ion batteries. They are light and hold a lot of energy, and they have become much cheaper. But they use metals like lithium, cobalt and nickel that are mined in only a few countries, and they can catch fire if damaged.

So scientists are working on new kinds. Sodium-ion batteries use sodium, a cheap [[element|element]] found in salt. Solid-state batteries replace the liquid inside with a solid, which could make them safer and hold more energy. Iron-air batteries could store electricity from wind and sun for days. The future will probably have many types, each for a different job.

st.prompt: One new type of battery stores energy for days by doing something iron does naturally. What is it?

options.t: Rusting and then turning back into iron
Melting and freezing
Getting magnetised

st.reveal: An iron-air battery lets tiny iron pellets react with oxygen and rust, which releases electricity. Charging it pushes the oxygen back out, turning the rust into iron again. It's heavy, so it's no good for phones, but iron is cheap, which suits giant batteries for power grids.

myth: You should let your phone battery run down to zero before charging it.
That advice was true for some older types of battery. Lithium-ion batteries actually last longer if you keep them between about 20% and 80% and avoid draining them completely.

sec.t:
Every battery has two ends, called electrodes, separated by a material called an [[electrolyte|electrolyte]]. When you use the battery, tiny charged particles called ions travel through the electrolyte from one electrode to the other. At the same time, [[electron|electrons]] flow through the wire outside, powering your device. Charging pushes everything back the other way.

Lithium is the lightest metal, and its ions are small and move easily. That is why lithium-ion batteries hold so much energy for their weight. In 2019, John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing them.

Sodium sits just below lithium in the periodic table and behaves in a similar way. It is far more plentiful, since there is a huge amount of it in seawater and rock salt. Sodium-ion batteries hold less energy than the best lithium ones, but they cost less and work better in the cold. By 2025, Chinese companies were putting them in some small cars and electric scooters.

Solid-state batteries swap the flammable liquid electrolyte for a solid, such as a special ceramic. They could charge faster and be safer, but making them reliably in large numbers is hard. Several carmakers say they hope to sell cars with them around the end of this decade.

Iron-air batteries are heavy but very cheap. They are being tested by power companies in the USA to store electricity for around 100 hours, enough to cover several cloudy, windless days.

India wants millions of electric vehicles, but it has had to [[import|import]] almost all its lithium. In 2023, the Geological Survey of India announced a lithium deposit estimated at about 5.9 million tonnes in Reasi, Jammu and Kashmir. It is still being studied, and it is not yet clear how much can be mined. India is also building large battery factories of its own.

When a battery wears out, its metals don't vanish. Recycling plants can recover lithium, cobalt, nickel and copper and use them to make new batteries. Car batteries that are too tired for driving can still store power for buildings for years.

Batteries thrown into ordinary rubbish can cause fires in garbage trucks and leak harmful materials, which is part of the problem of [[@e-waste|e-waste]]. Many scientists think the battery of the future will be designed from the start to be easy to take apart and reuse.

text: Lab-grown meat, also called cultivated meat, is real meat grown from animal cells outside an animal's body. Scientists take a few cells from a cow, chicken or fish, then feed them in a warm tank so they multiply into billions. The result is muscle and fat, the same stuff as a chicken nugget, without raising and killing the bird.

It is not science fiction any more. Singapore approved the first sales in 2020, the USA followed in 2023, and a few other countries have since joined. But it is still very expensive and hard to find in shops.

st.reveal: Scientists can take a tiny sample of muscle from a living animal with a needle, a bit like a blood test. Those cells can be kept and multiplied for a very long time.

sec.t:
Every animal is built from cells. Muscle cells, given food, warmth and a safe place, can divide again and again. Scientists put them in a steel tank called a bioreactor, a bit like a giant pressure cooker that keeps everything clean and at body temperature.

The cells float in a broth of sugars, salts, amino [[acid|acids]] and [[vitamin|vitamins]]. In a few weeks, a small sample can multiply into a large mass. For minced meat, that mass is harvested and shaped. For something like a steak, cells need a scaffold, a kind of edible sponge, so they grow in layers like real muscle. That part is much harder.

Supporters point to the numbers. About 80 billion land animals are killed for food every year worldwide. Cows release methane, a gas that warms the planet, and farming uses huge areas of land and water. Growing only the meat, without the rest of the animal, could need far less land and spare animals' lives.

That last point has interested some people in India, where many families avoid meat for religious or moral reasons. Some ask whether lab-grown meat would count as vegetarian. Most say no, since it is still animal flesh. India had not approved any lab-grown meat for sale as of 2025, though some Indian startups are working on it.

Critics say the [[climate|climate]] benefits are not proven. Big bioreactors use a lot of electricity, and if that power comes from coal, the meat might not be greener at all. Early methods also used a liquid taken from unborn calves to feed the cells. Most companies now say they have replaced it.

Some farmers fear for their jobs. In the USA, Florida and Alabama banned the sale of lab-grown meat in 2024. By mid-2025, at least seven states had banned or paused it. Supporters call the bans unfair. Opponents say people deserve time to see if it is safe.

The idea of growing food with tiny living things is not new, though. Humans have used [[microbe|microbes]] to make curd, bread and dosa batter for thousands of years, through [[@fermentation|fermentation]]. Lab meat may still find its place on our plates beside dals and [[@vegetarian|vegetarian]] curries. What it might share the menu with by 2050, from insects to seaweed, is the story of [[@future-food|future food]].

text: A games console is a computer built for one job: running games smoothly on a TV. Inside are a few key parts. The CPU is the brain that follows the game's rules. The GPU is a graphics chip that draws the pictures. Memory holds what the game needs right now, and storage keeps the game itself.

You press a button on the controller. The CPU works out what happens, maybe your character jumps. The GPU then draws the new scene, and the console sends it to the screen. This loop repeats 30, 60 or even 120 times every second, so smoothly that it feels like a moving world.

st.prompt: In a fast game, about how many fresh pictures does a console draw on the screen every second?

options.t: About 2
About 60
About 5,000

st.reveal: Many games draw 30 or 60 complete frames a second, and some aim for 120. Each frame is worked out from scratch, so the console has only a few thousandths of a second to draw every one.

sec.t:
The CPU handles the thinking. It checks where every enemy is, whether you hit the ball, and what the physics says should happen when a car crashes.

The GPU is the artist. Modern game worlds are built from millions of tiny triangles. For every frame, the GPU works out where each triangle sits, how light falls on it and what colour every [[@pixels|pixel]] should be. A GPU has thousands of small processing cores working side by side, all built on [[@chips-silicon|silicon chips]] with billions of tiny switches.

sec.h: From one dot to whole worlds

sec.t:
The computer that guided Apollo astronauts to the [[@apollo-moon|Moon]] in 1969 had about 4 kilobytes of working memory. A PlayStation 5 has 16 gigabytes. That is roughly four million times more.

All of it is stored as [[@binary-code|binary code]], long strings of 1s and 0s. A big modern game can take up over 100 gigabytes, about as much as the plain text of 100,000 novels.

A controller is a small computer of its own. Each button closes a tiny electrical [[circuit|circuit]] when pressed. The thumbsticks measure how far you push them, many times a second, and send those numbers to the console by wire or radio.

Many controllers also hide little motors with off-centre weights. When they spin, the controller rumbles, so you feel a crash or an explosion as well as seeing it. Some newer ones can tighten their triggers, so pulling a bowstring in a game really feels harder.

sec.h: Why consoles are so cheap for what they do
sec.t:
Building a gaming computer with the same power often costs more than a console. Console makers sometimes sell the machine at little or no profit, then earn money on games, subscriptions and online services.

Because every copy of a console is identical, game makers know exactly what hardware they are writing for. That lets them squeeze out performance a general computer can't always match.

As of 2026, the best-selling console ever is still Sony's PlayStation 2 from 2000, with about 160 million sold. The original Nintendo Switch, launched in 2017, had reached about 156 million and was closing in. Its follow-up, the Switch 2, came out in 2025.

In 1990s India, few families could buy an official Nintendo. Instead, many homes had cheap copies of the Famicom, sold as "TV video games" with yellow cartridges claiming hundreds of games in one. Lots of those games were the same handful repeated. Children still played them for hours, humming the tunes that the story of [[@video-game-music|video game music]] explains.

text: Golconda is a huge [[granite|granite]] fort on a hill at the edge of Hyderabad. For about 170 years it was the capital of the Qutb Shahi sultans, one of the richest kingdoms in the world. Its wealth came from diamonds dug from mines in the surrounding region.

The fort is famous for clever engineering. Its walls run for kilometres, with 87 bastions and eight gates. Water was lifted to the hilltop. And its builders designed the entrance so that a single handclap could warn the guards at the top.
In 1687 the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb captured it after a long siege. The diamonds' fame lives on in its name.

st.reveal: Aurangzeb's army besieged the fort for about eight months. Cannons and mines failed to break it. In the end, according to the usual account, an officer inside was bribed to open a gate.

sec.h: From a shepherd's hill to a sultan's fort
sec.t:
A local story says the name comes from Golla Konda, meaning "shepherd's hill" in Telugu. A shepherd boy is said to have found a sacred idol there. The first fort on the hill was a mud fort built under the [[@kakatiyas|Kakatiya]] kings of Warangal.

In 1518, a governor named Sultan Quli Qutb-ul-Mulk declared his own kingdom. His family, the Qutb Shahis, turned the mud fort into a stone city with palaces, mosques, armouries, gardens and homes. Thousands of people lived inside the outer walls.

The fort grew so crowded that in 1591 Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah founded a new city nearby. Its centrepiece was the [[@charminar|Charminar]]. That city became Hyderabad.

The main entrance is called the Fateh Darwaza, the Victory Gate. Its huge wooden doors are studded with iron spikes to stop war elephants from ramming them.

Stand under the dome near the gate and clap, and the sound travels up to the Bala Hissar pavilion at the very top of the hill, about a kilometre away. Guards could use it as an alarm. Hard stone surfaces bounce sound, the same way [[@echoes|echoes]] do in a big empty hall.

Visitors still try it today. Guides clap, and someone at the top shouts back. It works best early in the morning, before the crowds and traffic noise of a big city drown out the clap.

{{story:charminar}}

For centuries, mines near the Krishna river, such as Kollur, produced some of the most famous diamonds on Earth. Golconda was where they were traded and guarded. Merchants travelled from Persia and Europe to buy them.

The [[@kohinoor|Koh-i-Noor]] is believed to have come from these mines. So is the deep-blue Hope Diamond, now in the Smithsonian museum in Washington, DC, and the pink Darya-i-Noor in Iran. Diamonds form deep underground under great heat and pressure, as you can see in [[@gems-crystals|how gems form]].

Golconda's fame was so great that its name entered English. A "golconda" means a mine of riches, a place of endless wealth.

Getting water to the top of a granite hill was a huge challenge. The builders made tanks to catch rainwater. They also used Persian wheels, chains of pots turned by animals, to lift water through clay pipes, stage by stage, up to the palaces.

The fort had its own [[reservoir|reservoirs]], so it could survive long sieges. That was tested in 1687. Aurangzeb's army surrounded Golconda for about eight months. The walls held. Then, according to the usual account, an officer named Abdullah Khan Pani was bribed to open a gate at night. The last Qutb Shahi sultan, Abul Hasan Tana Shah, was taken prisoner.

Near the fort stand the Qutb Shahi Tombs, a garden of domed tombs of the sultans. And the strangest part? The city born from Golconda's crowds grew into one of India's biggest, whose story continues in [[@hyderabad|Hyderabad]].

text: The Great Depression was the worst economic slump of the modern world. It began in the United States in 1929 and lasted through most of the 1930s. Factories closed, banks failed, and millions of people lost their jobs, savings and homes.

Because countries traded and lent money to each other, the trouble spread fast. Farmers in Brazil, factory workers in Germany and jute growers in Bengal all felt it. Governments tried different cures. Some worked, some made things worse, and the hard times helped bring dangerous leaders to power.

They crashed, so farmers earned far less

st.reveal: With so many people out of work, demand fell and crop prices collapsed. Farmers in places as far apart as Kansas and Punjab earned much less for the same harvest, but still had to pay their rent, debts and taxes.

n.certNote: Everyone agrees on what happened, but economists still argue about why the slump was so deep and so long. Some blame banks and the money supply, others falling spending and trade barriers.

sec.t:
In the 1920s many Americans bought shares in companies, often with borrowed money, betting that prices would keep rising. Prices on the [[@stock-market|stock market]] soared far beyond what the companies were really worth.

In late October 1929 the bubble burst. On 24 October, later called Black Thursday, panicked owners rushed to sell. Five days later came Black Tuesday, when prices fell even further. Fortunes vanished in days. The crash did not cause the whole Depression on its own, but it shook people's confidence and made them stop spending.

sec.h: When banks ran out of money

sec.t:
On the Great Plains, farmers faced a second disaster. Years of ploughing had stripped away the grass that held the soil down. When [[@droughts|drought]] struck in the 1930s, the wind lifted the dry topsoil into giant black clouds. Some [[@usa-dust-bowl|dust storms]] rolled hundreds of kilometres and dropped dirt as far east as the Atlantic coast.

Hundreds of thousands of people left the Plains, many heading west to California to look for work. The writer John Steinbeck told their story in his novel *The Grapes of Wrath*.

In 1933 Franklin D. Roosevelt became president and promised a "New Deal". The government hired millions of people to build roads, dams, schools and parks. One programme, the Civilian Conservation Corps, gave jobs to young men who planted about three billion trees across the country. New rules protected bank savings. In 1935 the Social Security Act began paying pensions to older Americans, a system that still exists.

Unemployment fell, but did not fully recover until factories got busy again near the start of the Second World War.

Countries tried to protect their own industries by putting big taxes on [[import|imports]]. That shrank world trade even more. In Germany, mass unemployment helped Adolf Hitler's Nazi party gain support, a step on the road to [[@world-war-two|World War Two]].

In India, prices for crops such as wheat, rice and jute fell by about half, but taxes and rents did not. Many farming families sold their gold jewellery to get by, and large amounts of gold flowed out of the country. Anger over these hardships fed into the freedom movement of the 1930s.

text: In [[medieval|medieval]] Europe, roughly 1000 to 1500 CE, castles were the fortified homes of kings and lords. They were part [[fortress|fortress]] and part house, and a lot of people lived inside.

Life in a castle was busy, noisy and often uncomfortable. The lord's family, knights, servants, cooks, grooms and soldiers all shared the space. Most people ate and some slept in a big room called the great hall, warmed by a fire whose smoke stung the eyes. Floors were covered with rushes, a kind of dried reed. Windows were small, to keep out arrows and cold. The toilets dropped waste down the walls. Castles also ran farms and courts, and they were where the local lord kept order.

Into pipes leading to a sewer under the town

st.reveal: Many garderobes were little stone seats built over a shaft in the outer wall. Waste dropped into the moat or a pit below, and servants had to clean it out. Some people hung clothes nearby, believing the smell kept moths away.

The first castles were quick to build. Soldiers piled earth into a mound, called a motte, and put a wooden tower on top. A fenced yard, the bailey, sat below.

After William of Normandy conquered England in 1066, the Normans built hundreds of these. Wood burns, so lords soon switched to stone. The White Tower at the Tower of [[@london|London]], begun around 1078, has walls up to about 4.5 metres thick at the base. Later castles added rings of walls, towers and gatehouses with iron gates called portcullises.

sec.t:
Knights were trained fighters on horseback who served a lord in return for land, part of a system historians call [[feudalism|feudalism]]. A boy from a noble family might start as a page at about seven, serving at table and learning manners.

At around fourteen he became a squire, caring for a knight's horse and armour and following him to battle. If he did well, he could be knighted around 21, in a ceremony called dubbing. Knights were expected to follow a code of honour called chivalry, though many did not.

Early knights wore chain mail, a shirt of thousands of linked iron rings. By the 1400s, rich knights wore full plate armour weighing roughly 15 to 25 kg. Because the weight was spread out, they could move quite freely.

To attack castles, armies used battering rams, siege towers and the trebuchet, a giant throwing machine. It used a heavy counterweight on a long arm, working like a [[@lever-lift|lever]], to hurl stones at walls. Often, though, attackers simply surrounded a castle and waited for its food to run out.

In the 1400s, cannons became powerful enough to smash high stone walls. Kings grew stronger, and lords no longer needed private fortresses.

Castles turned into palaces, prisons, ruins or tourist sites. India has its own great forts, such as Mehrangarh in Jodhpur, begun in 1459 on a rocky hill about 120 metres above the city, and the Maratha hill forts of [[@shivaji|Shivaji]]. Japan built tall white castles for its [[@samurai|samurai]] lords. Around the world, people facing similar dangers came up with surprisingly similar answers.

text: Magna Carta, Latin for "Great Charter", is an agreement between King John of England and a group of rebel barons. It was made on 15 June 1215, at a meadow called Runnymede beside the River Thames. Its main idea was that the king, too, had to follow the law.

Most of its 63 clauses dealt with problems of the time, such as taxes, forests and the rights of barons. The agreement quickly fell apart. Yet a few clauses, especially the promise of fair justice, became famous. Over the centuries, people in England, the United States, India and elsewhere pointed to Magna Carta when they argued for rights and limits on power.

About ten years
About a hundred years

st.reveal: King John asked Pope Innocent III to cancel the charter, and the Pope did so in August 1215, about ten weeks later. War broke out, but after John died, new versions of the charter were issued in 1216, 1217 and 1225.
