Most of its promises were for "free men", mainly barons, knights and churchmen. Most ordinary people at the time were serfs, called villeins, who were not free and gained little from it.

sec.t:
King John was unpopular. He had lost most of England's lands in France, and he raised huge taxes from his barons to pay for wars to win them back. He also punished people without fair trials and quarrelled with the Pope.

In 1215 many barons rebelled and captured [[@london|London]]. John agreed to meet them at Runnymede, between his castle at Windsor and the rebel camp. There he set his seal on a document listing their demands. Copies were written out by hand in Latin and sent around the kingdom.

Most clauses are long out of date. One deals with fish weirs in rivers, another with debts owed to moneylenders. Only three clauses are still part of English law today.

The most famous lines were later joined into a single clause. In modern English, they say that no free man shall be arrested, imprisoned or punished "except by the lawful judgement of his equals or by the law of the land". They go on: "To no one will we sell, to no one deny or delay right or justice."

These lines express ideas still at the heart of many legal systems: a fair trial, and a government that must follow the [[@laws-made|law]].

English settlers carried the idea of Magna Carta to America. When the colonists rebelled against Britain in the 1770s, they argued that the king was denying them rights that went back to 1215.

The [[@us-constitution|US Constitution]] and its Bill of Rights promise that no person shall be "deprived of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law", words that trace back to Magna Carta. In 1957, the American Bar Association built a memorial at Runnymede. A copy of Magna Carta from 1297 is on display in the National Archives in Washington, D.C.

Four original copies from 1215 survive. Two are in the British Library in London, one in Lincoln Castle and one in Salisbury Cathedral. They are written in tiny, neat Latin on a single sheet of parchment, made from animal skin.

In India, the idea that no one can be deprived of life or liberty except according to law is part of Article 21 of the [[@constitution|Constitution]]. The meadow at Runnymede is now looked after by the National Trust, and visitors can walk where the barons and the king once faced each other.

text: Vallabhbhai Patel was a lawyer from Gujarat who became one of the toughest leaders of India's [[@freedom-struggle|freedom struggle]]. After independence in 1947 he was Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister.

His biggest task was a puzzle. British India was only part of the [[subcontinent|subcontinent]]. The rest was made up of more than 560 [[@princely-states|princely states]], kingdoms ruled by maharajas, nawabs and nizams. When the British left, each ruler could in theory stay independent. Patel and his secretary V.P. Menon persuaded, bargained with and sometimes pressured nearly all of them to join India. Without this, India's map could have looked like a quilt with holes.

All their land and palaces

st.reveal: The Instrument of Accession asked only for three things at first, defence, foreign affairs and communications. Rulers kept their titles and were promised allowances. Asking for little made it easier for most to say yes.

sec.h: A farmer's son who became chief
sec.t:
Patel was born in 1875 into a farming family in Nadiad. He studied law, saved money for years, and finally went to London to qualify as a barrister. He finished the course early and came top of his class. Back home he became a successful lawyer in Ahmedabad, sharp, well dressed and impatient with what he saw as idealistic talk.

That changed when he met [[@gandhi|Gandhi]]. Patel organised farmers in Kheda in 1918 to refuse taxes after their crops failed. In 1928 he led farmers in Bardoli against a steep tax rise. The government backed down, and the people of Bardoli began calling him "Sardar", chief.

Some princely states were tiny, just a few villages. Others were larger than many European countries. Hyderabad alone had more people than Britain's Scotland and Wales put together.

Patel offered the rulers a deal called the Instrument of Accession. They would hand over defence, foreign affairs and communications, and keep their titles and a yearly allowance. He appealed to their patriotism, met many of them himself, and made it clear that India's people wanted unity.

{{story:states-india}}

By 15 August 1947, almost every state had signed. Over the next two years, many small states were also merged into larger units, which later became today's states.

Three states held out. The Nawab of Junagadh in Gujarat chose Pakistan, though most of his people were Hindu and the state was surrounded by India. After a public vote in February 1948, Junagadh joined India.

[[@hyderabad|Hyderabad]], ruled by the Nizam, wanted to stay independent. In September 1948 Indian troops entered in an operation that lasted about four days, and Hyderabad joined India.

The Maharaja of Kashmir signed the Instrument of Accession in October 1947 as raiders from Pakistan attacked. Indian troops were flown in to defend Srinagar. The dispute over Kashmir continues to this day, and [[@nehru|Nehru]], more than Patel, handled it in the years that followed.

Patel also defended the civil services, the officers who run districts and departments. Some leaders wanted to scrap a system the British had built. Patel argued that free India needed trained, neutral officers. He called them the country's "steel frame", and today's IAS and IPS grew from his decision.

Patel died on 15 December 1950, only three years after independence. He is remembered as the Iron Man of India, firm and practical. Since 2014 his birthday, 31 October, has been marked as National Unity Day.

His face now looks out over the Narmada river from the [[@statue-of-unity|Statue of Unity]], the tallest statue on Earth. A quieter memorial and museum to him stands in the Moti Shahi Mahal palace in Ahmedabad.

text: Mount Kilimanjaro is the highest mountain in Africa, at 5,895 m. It rises alone from the plains of northern Tanzania, near the border with Kenya. Unlike the Himalayas, it isn't part of a range. It's a giant volcano, built up by eruptions over hundreds of thousands of years.

From the dry grassland at its foot, it climbs almost 5 km into the sky. That makes it one of the tallest free-standing mountains on Earth. Every year tens of thousands of people try to walk to the summit. You need no ropes or climbing gear on the main routes, but you do need patience, warm clothes and lungs that can cope with thin air.

st.prompt: Climbers on Kilimanjaro pass through many kinds of landscape in a few days. What is the climb often compared to?

options.t: Walking from the equator to the Arctic
Crossing a desert to reach the sea
Going from a city to a village

st.reveal: The trail starts among farms and rainforest, then rises through heath and moorland, then a dry, stony alpine desert. Near the top it is freezing, with ice and snow. Every 1,000 m you climb, the air gets roughly 6 °C colder.

n.certNote: The mountain's height and history are well known. Scientists agree its glaciers are shrinking fast, but estimates of when they will disappear range from the 2030s to the 2050s, and they disagree about how much is due to global warming and how much to drier air.

sec.t:
Kilimanjaro is made of three volcanic cones. Shira, in the west, is the oldest and has mostly worn away. Mawenzi, in the east, is a jagged, broken peak. Kibo, in the middle, is the youngest and tallest, and its [[crater|crater]] rim holds Uhuru Peak, the highest point.

Nobody is quite sure where the name Kilimanjaro comes from, though several Swahili and Chagga meanings have been suggested.

Kibo is dormant, not dead. It hasn't erupted for a very long time, but there are still vents near the summit where gas seeps out. The mountain grew as part of the forces that are slowly pulling East Africa apart, the same ones that formed the [[@great-rift-valley|Great Rift Valley]].

Climbing Kilimanjaro is like travelling from the [[equator|equator]] to the Arctic in a week. The lower slopes are farmland, where the Chagga people grow bananas and coffee. Above that is thick rainforest with colobus monkeys. Higher still come heath and moorland, then a stony alpine desert with almost no plants.

At the summit, nights fall far below freezing. Strange plants grow on the way up, including giant groundsels that look like cabbages on tree trunks and can be taller than a person.

In 1912, ice covered much of Kibo's summit. Since then more than 80% has vanished. Some of the remaining [[glacier|glaciers]] look like white cliffs standing on brown rock.

Scientists study why. Warmer temperatures play a part. So does drier air, which means less snow falls to replace the ice, and strong sunshine that turns ice straight into water vapour. Many expect the last of Kilimanjaro's ice to disappear within a few decades.

The writer Ernest Hemingway made the mountain famous in 1936 with a story called "The Snows of Kilimanjaro". Children climbing it in the future may find only bare rock at the top. For the people on its slopes, the bigger worry is water. The melting [[@glaciers|glaciers]] supply only a little of it. The forests matter more, because they catch rain and mist and feed the streams that farms depend on, so protecting those trees has become a big part of caring for the mountain.

text: Niagara Falls formed at the end of the last [[@ice-ages|ice age]], about 12,000 years ago. Thick ice sheets had covered the area and carved out the [[@great-lakes|Great Lakes]]. As the ice melted, water from Lake Erie began flowing north to Lake Ontario through the Niagara River. On the way, it tumbled over a steep cliff of rock called the Niagara Escarpment.
At first the falls were near where the towns of Lewiston and Queenston stand today. Since then, the water has worn away the rock and pushed the falls about 11 km upriver, leaving a deep gorge behind.

sec.h: A hard lid on soft rock
sec.t:
The secret of Niagara lies in its layers of [[@rocks-types|rock]]. At the top is a hard rock called dolostone. Underneath are softer layers of shale and sandstone. The falling water churns at the bottom and scours away the soft rock, leaving the hard top layer hanging out over empty space. In time, the overhang cracks and falls, and the edge moves back.

This used to happen fast, about a metre a year. Today much of the river's water is taken out before it reaches the falls, to make [[@electricity-made|electricity]], so the [[erosion|erosion]] is much slower.

Niagara is really three waterfalls on the border between Canada and the USA. The biggest is the Horseshoe Falls, mostly in Canada, about 51 m high and curved like a horseshoe. The American Falls and the small Bridal Veil Falls lie on the US side, separated by Goat Island.

In the tourist season, up to about 2,800 cubic metres of water pour over the falls every second during the day. That would fill an Olympic swimming pool in about one second. At night, a [[treaty|treaty]] between Canada and the USA lets power companies take even more water.

Water falling that far carries a huge amount of energy. In 1895, a power station opened at Niagara using alternating current, a system developed by [[@nikola-tesla|Nikola Tesla]] and built with the Westinghouse company. In 1896, it sent electricity about 40 km to the city of Buffalo. It was one of the first big [[@renewable-energy|hydroelectric plants]] in the world, and it showed how [[@dams-power|falling water could power]] whole cities.

{{story:nikola-tesla}}

By the 1960s, piles of fallen rock were building up at the foot of the American Falls. In 1969, the US Army Corps of Engineers built a temporary dam upstream and turned the American Falls off for about five months. Visitors walked on the dry riverbed. Engineers and [[geologist|geologists]] studied the rocks and cracks. In the end, they decided to let nature take its course and reopened the falls.

Niagara has always drawn daredevils. In 1859, Charles Blondin walked across the gorge on a tightrope. In 1901, Annie Edson Taylor, a 63-year-old teacher, went over the Horseshoe Falls in a wooden barrel and survived. [[@behind-stunts|Stunts like hers]] are now against the law.

Since 1846, boats have carried visitors close to the bottom of the falls, into the thundering spray. Passengers wear raincoats, and still come back soaked.

In very cold winters, spray freezes onto rocks, trees and railings, coating them in thick ice. Huge mounds of ice, called ice bridges, can form at the bottom. People once walked across them, until a deadly collapse in 1912 led to a ban. On sunny days the mist rising from the falls catches the light, and [[@rainbow-how|rainbows]] hang over the gorge for hours.

text: The coconut palm is called the tree of life because almost every part of it is useful. The water inside a young coconut is a refreshing drink. The white flesh is eaten fresh, grated into curries, or squeezed to make coconut milk. Dried flesh is pressed for oil, used in cooking and on hair.

The tough husk gives coir fibre for ropes, mats and brushes. The hard shells become cups, spoons and fuel. The leaves are woven into roofs, mats and baskets, and their midribs are tied into brooms. The trunks are used as timber. In Kerala, the palm is called kalpavriksha, the tree that grants every wish.

sec.h: A seed built for the sea

sec.t: Despite its name, a coconut isn't a true nut. [[botanist|Botanists]] call it a drupe, a fruit with a fleshy or fibrous outer layer and a hard stone inside. Mangoes, peaches and cherries are drupes too. In a coconut, the outer layer is the husk, and the "stone" is the brown shell we usually see in shops.

Coconut palms love warm, wet, coastal places. [[@bali|Indonesia]], the Philippines and India are among the world's biggest producers. In India, Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh grow the most.

On India's [[@coral-reefs|coral]] islands of [[@lakshadweep|Lakshadweep]], coconut palms are everywhere, and coconut is central to food and income. Studies of coconut DNA suggest that cultivated coconuts were developed separately in two regions, one around the Pacific and one around the Indian Ocean.

In South India and along the western coast, coconut is in almost everything. Grated coconut goes into thoran and poriyal. Coconut milk makes stews and curries creamy. Coconut chutney is served with idli and dosa. Kerala cooks fry many dishes in [[@oils-cooking|coconut oil]].

Sweets use coconut too, from Maharashtra's modak to Goa's [[@goan-food|bebinca]]. Tender coconut water is sold on beaches and roadsides, often by vendors who slice the top off with a few swift strokes.

Coconuts play a big part in Hindu [[ritual|rituals]]. Breaking a coconut is a common offering at temples and at the start of new ventures, from opening a shop to launching a ship. In Maharashtra, fishing communities celebrate Narali Purnima by offering coconuts to the sea before the fishing season begins.

The husk fibre, called coir, is soaked, beaten and spun into strong, rough rope. Coir mats and ropes are made in large numbers in Kerala, especially around Alappuzha. Coir resists salt water, so it was traditionally used for ships' ropes and fishing nets.

Weavers twist and [[@weaving-saree|weave]] coir into doormats, carpets and even mattresses. Nothing from the palm goes to waste, which is why it earned its name.
